article_core: The 1892 expedition was a mobile intervention inside an already distributed Harvard-Hosterwitz reference-production system. Before Rudolf travelled, Harvard and the workshop already exchanged plants, seeds, books, lists, catalogues and living nursery material across the Atlantic. The journey supplemented this remote supply ecology by changing the kinds and biological states of American reference material available to the workshop through direct field observation, cultivated access, drawings, living material, dried specimens, alcohol specimens and seeds. Field selection remained governed by ecological and seasonal availability, Harvard collection need/redundancy, access regime, identification confidence, desired biological state, medium feasibility, body/time/route constraints and a remotely administered budget. Returned material became workshop stock whose members could remain dormant for years while taxonomy, redundancy, difficulty, priority and capacity determined staged reactivation into glass models and later shipments. Finished models then entered distinct mounting, packing, customs, receiving, repair and installation chains.
major_revision_from_pass35: American access now begins before 1892 in the analytical chronology. The December 1891 claim that some forms were 'hitherto inaccessible' is read against documented 1889-1891 remote supply, so inaccessibility is treated as residual and state-specific rather than a blanket geographical condition.

gate_B.principle: The expedition returned as stock, not as a shipment plan. Journey provenance did not confer automatic production priority. Reference material could remain secured for years while taxonomy, collection saturation and workshop difficulty changed around it.

supply_and_access_regimes.remote_contractual_supply: By 1889 Harvard was contractually responsible for providing plants, seeds and books and for supporting care of American plants at Hosterwitz. A circulating American-plant list is explicit in February 1890, and Gillett & Horsford supplied living California material by 1890.
supply_and_access_regimes.commercial_nursery_mediation: Southwick catalogues and living plant shipments could move American material to Dresden before field travel; the workshop then cultivated, compared and sometimes modelled material despite unresolved determination.
supply_and_access_regimes.institutional_compression: Botanical gardens can concentrate named cultivated plants, specialists, lodging coordination and work space; St Louis converts Darlingtonia into same-day colour-sketch and alcohol-reference capture.
supply_and_access_regimes.ecological_extension: Wild excursions expand the local reference set and preserve direct habitat encounter; institutional access and field search can operate on the same stop.
supply_and_access_regimes.mobile_field_acquisition: The 1892 journey adds direct observation and reference states poorly supplied remotely: flowering/fruiting condition, colour, habitat, living morphology, dried or alcohol-preserved structures and opportunistic seeds.
supply_and_access_regimes.later_gap_filling: After the journey, locally obtainable cultivated or nursery material could fill collection gaps when journey stock was redundant, inadequate or unavailable.

governance_lanes.communication: Letters, telegrams, lists, catalogues and reference packets move collection needs, field status, patron instructions, route decisions and material between Cambridge, suppliers, the travelling party and Hosterwitz.

collection_saturation_claim: The 1901 filler-scarcity evidence shows that the collection itself produced a changing economy of difficulty. As easy non-redundant subjects disappeared, remaining useful additions became disproportionately difficult. A growing collection changes the cost structure of the next useful model.

working_claims: The collection travelled twice: through objects moving toward Cambridge/Hosterwitz and through portable descriptions of what the collection still lacked.
The expedition returned as stock, not as a shipment plan.
The expedition did not inaugurate American access; it altered the kinds and states of reference material available inside an older supply ecology.
Remote supply and fieldwork were complementary access regimes.
Inaccessibility was relative to the biological and epistemic state required for modelling, not geography alone.
Botanical gardens compressed botanical access; field excursions extended it; nurseries could fill residual gaps across time.
A jar, a boarding arrangement, a nursery catalogue and a railway diversion belonged to the same operational system because each changed what could become a usable reference.

Harvard governed the expedition without directing it minute by minute: it maintained balances, transmitted priorities, supplied reference infrastructure, authorized facilities and answered exceptional route decisions while Rudolf and Ganong retained local discretion.
A growing collection changes the cost structure of the next useful model.
